title: Hexagonal architecture
idea: Hexagonal architecture keeps business logic in a core that talks to the outside only through interfaces it owns, called ports; adapters plug technologies into them.

analogy.text: A laptop has standard ports. Chargers, screens and drives from any brand plug in through adapters. The laptop never changes to suit a new device.
analogy.breaks: Hardware ports are fixed standards; your ports are interfaces you design and evolve.

points: Driving ports are use cases the core offers; HTTP or CLI adapters call them.
Driven ports are what the core needs, like storage; database adapters implement them.
Every dependency points inward: adapters know the core, the core knows no adapter.
One composition root wires adapters, so tests swap a database for an in-memory fake.

steps.caption: An HTTP request arrives. The adapter parses JSON; that technology detail stays here.
The adapter calls the driving port with a plain `String`. No HTTP types cross the line.
The core validates the url and asks a generator for a code. Business rules live only here.
The core saves through `LinkStore`, an interface it owns. It does not know which store is wired.
The driven adapter implements the port. Swapping in a SQL store changes this box only.
`save` returns. The core hands the code back through its driving port.
The HTTP adapter turns the result into a 201 response. A bad url would become a 400 here.

code.title: Core, ports and two adapters
code.caption: A CLI adapter and an HTTP adapter drive the same core. Each maps the same domain error to its own format.

walk.text: Ports are interfaces in the core's own terms: one driving port, two driven ports.
The core holds the rules and depends only on ports, injected through the constructor.
A domain exception says what went wrong, not how to show it.
The CLI adapter parses text and turns the domain error into a message line.
The HTTP adapter maps the same error to a 400. The core never sees status codes.
Driven adapters implement the core's ports; a SQL store would replace only these.
The composition root is the one place that picks concrete adapters.

code.title: Testing the core with fakes
code.caption: The same core runs with a recording store and a lambda generator. No server, no database, no mocks library.

walk.text: Test adapters plug into the driven ports; a lambda is enough for a one-method port.
Assert on what crossed the port, not on any private field of the core.
The failure path is tested too: a bad url throws and saves nothing.
A tiny `check` runner stands in for JUnit 5, which this book cannot load.
The fake records calls in order, so the test result is deterministic.

pitfalls: Putting JPA or Jackson annotations on domain classes: the core now depends on an adapter technology.
Defining ports in the adapter package: the arrow flips and the core imports infrastructure.
One port per table with CRUD methods: ports should name what the core needs, like `findExpiredLinks`.

quiz.q: Your team moves link storage from memory to PostgreSQL. In a clean hexagon, what changes?
options: A new `LinkStore` adapter and the composition root
Every driving adapter, since they reach the database
Nothing; the core opens the connection itself
quiz.why: The core depends only on the `LinkStore` port. You add an adapter implementing it and wire it in the composition root; core and driving adapters stay untouched.

takeaway: The core owns the ports; adapters depend on the core, never the reverse.

starters: How is hexagonal architecture different from a layered architecture?
Where do DTOs and mapping live in ports and adapters?
